entities.name: Jean-Antoine Roucher
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jean-Antoine Roucher (1745–1794) was a French poet of the late Enlightenment whose pastoral and descriptive verse earned contemporary esteem before the Revolution engulfed him. Associated with the cultivated provincial and Parisian literary world, he wrote in a refined classical idiom celebrating nature, friendship, and moral sensibility.

During the Revolution Roucher’s moderate or suspect political stance led to imprisonment; he was guillotined in 1794 during the Terror, reportedly sharing a cart with André Chénier in later commemorative tradition. His death made him a martyr figure for readers who mourned the Revolution’s destruction of men of letters.

Literary history remembers Roucher as both a late-Ancien Régime descriptive poet and a symbolic victim of revolutionary violence against the republic of letters.
